newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Privatisation vital to Bulgarian reform - agency.
newsitem.headline: Privatisation vital to Bulgarian reform - agency.

text.p: Bulgaria's Privatisation Agency is accelerating sell-offs to reform troubled state companies and generate vital revenue for the state budget, executive director Alexander Sabotinov said on Wednesday.

Privatisation will be a key source of income for the government after it is cut off from central bank lending under a currency board regime, a restrictive monetary policy tool of the central bank due to be introduced in June.

"We want to accelerate cash privatisation to improve the conditions, to shorten the period of time and to open the privatisation procedure to the public to improve transparency," Sabotinov told Reuters Television in an interview.
The Agency announced last month it was seeking financial advisers for privatisation of 22 large state companies.
A thorough restructuring of the state sector is one condition of a $657 million reform and funding agreement approved by the International Monetary Fund last Friday.

"Our urgent task for this moment is to select a first five companies for quick privatisation," said Sabotinov, who was appointed on April 1 after the Agency's supervisory board sacked the previous executive director.

He said the five companies would be selected in the next few days and could include Dyuni tourist resort, Verila chemical company, Agrobiochim bio-products company, Asarel-Medet copper refinery, and drugs firm Antibiotic.
Sabotinov said big communist-era companies like Neftochim refinery, Kremikovtsi steelworks and the National Electricity Company were candidates for restructuring and partial privatisation.
"All these giants need transformation, privatisation, even sale of assets," he said.
One plan under consideration at the industry ministry is to float shares in state companies on a revived stock exchange to improve transparency and increase investor confidence.
On Tuesday, the Privatisation Agency announced completion of the sale of 60 percent of the Sodi soda ash plant to Belgium's Solvay for $160 million, Bulgaria's biggest sale so far.

Sabotinov said Daewoo Corp had shown interest in buying 60 percent of the Chimco chemical plant but its offer had not been high enough. "We met only one buyer and our expectations for the proposed offer price have not been met," he said.
He said the Agency had asked Daewoo if they were prepared to increase their offer, and if they declined, they would reopen the bidding.
Another difficult sell-off will be Balkan Airways, which is on the list of 22 firms. A previous privatisation attempt failed to find a buyer.

"I am not so optimistic but this time we have to use all possible schemes for privatisation, even through a capital increase, or transferring of know-how or some other intangible assets. The company is not in a good condition so we are open to discussing every proposal in this direction," Sabotinov said.
Also on the list is the indebted Neftochim refinery. The government plans to offer a 75 percent stake and Russia's Rosneft, its main supplier, has shown interest.
Sabotinov said a debt for equity deal would not be the best way to ensure the company modernised and improved its management.

"A better solution would be for the privatisation to be developed and implemented with participation of more than one investor. Only one (investor) cannot solve all the problems the company has," he said.
He said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell had started the first phase of consultancy work to prepare the privatisation of Bulgarian Telecommunications Company.
Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said on Tuesday said the state Greek Telecommunications Organisation (OTE) was among operators interested in the sale.
